findings.title: Respect parameter limits on PostgreSQL and MySQL
findings.body: The non-SQLite path creates one bound parameter per ID without capping the batch. PostgreSQL and prepared MySQL statements support at most 65,535 parameters, so a cleanup batch configured above that limit fails whenever enough eligible rows exist. The previous subquery-based DELETE did not have this restriction. Cleanup then returns without deleting the batch and fails again on subsequent runs, preventing retention cleanup from progressing. Cap or subdivide DELETE batches according to the database's parameter limit.

findings.title: Build the SQLite ID list without repeatedly copying it
findings.body: Each fmt.Sprintf copies the entire accumulated ID list into a new string, making construction allocate O(n²) bytes. A roughly 32,000-ID batch produces several gigabytes of transient allocations for a final SQL list of only a few hundred kilobytes. This specifically penalizes the large batches the SQLite fallback is intended to support, adding substantial CPU and garbage-collection work to cleanup. Use a strings.Builder or byte buffer to construct the list linearly.

findings.title: Do not report successful cleanup batches as errors
findings.body: The new annotation and tag cleanup paths call log.Error unconditionally after successful queries and deletes. This includes empty batches with no eligible rows and a nil error, so healthy scheduled cleanup now emits error-level messages on every run, often with an entire batch of IDs. This creates false failure signals for operators and error-based monitoring while adding unnecessary log volume. Remove these diagnostics or log them at Debug, reserving Error for actual failures.

findings.title: Preserve the cadence of the global cleanup scheduler
findings.body: This ticker controls all eight cleanup jobs, not just annotation cleanup. Changing it from ten minutes to one minute schedules database and filesystem cleanup ten times as often. The existing cleanup timeout remains nine minutes, so runs lasting longer than one minute can also leave a tick pending and restart immediately, making cleanup effectively continuous. This introduces a broad background-load regression unrelated to splitting the annotation SQL statements; retain the existing interval or schedule annotations separately if a faster cadence is required.
